🚩 Blood-handling hazard: re-injecting mislabelled cells into the wrong patient is potentially fatal. Rigorous single-patient identity checks, aseptic technique and universal precautions against blood-borne viruses are mandatory throughout separation, labelling and reinjection.
🎓 For suspected prosthetic joint infection or diabetic-foot osteomyelitis, always pair the labelled leucocyte scan with a ⁹⁹ᵐTc marrow scan: infection is uptake on the white-cell study that is NOT matched on the marrow map, which markedly improves specificity.

Lymphoscintigraphy maps the drainage of a tumour to its sentinel lymph node — the first node (or nodes) into which a tumour drains and therefore the first likely site of nodal metastasis. A ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled colloid is injected around the tumour or biopsy cavity, tracks through the lymphatics, and is trapped in the sentinel node, which is then localised by gamma imaging and, at surgery, by a hand-held gamma probe (usually combined with blue dye). It underpins sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) in breast cancer and melanoma, letting a node-negative patient avoid the morbidity of full nodal clearance.

☢️⁹⁹ᵐTc-nanocolloid
Small colloid particles enter lymphatics & are phagocytosed/trapped in the first draining node.
🔵Patent blue dye
Intra-operative visual co-localiser; stains the sentinel node & afferent lymphatic blue.
📡Gamma probe
Hand-held detector guides the surgeon to the “hot” node through a small incision.
🎯Sentinel node
First node draining the tumour — its status predicts the whole regional basin.
1Indications & rationale
Breast cancer — early invasive breast cancer with a clinically & radiologically node-negative axilla, to stage the axilla accurately.
Cutaneous melanoma — to stage the regional nodal basin (typically ≥ pT1b / thickness ≥ 0.8 mm with adverse features), guiding prognosis and adjuvant therapy.
The aim is to avoid unnecessary full nodal clearance (axillary dissection / block dissection) and its morbidity — chiefly lymphoedema, nerve injury and shoulder stiffness.
Sentinel node negative→no completion nodal dissection needed — basin spared
Sentinel node positive→guides further management (further nodal treatment, radiotherapy or surveillance)
2Technique & timing
Injection: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-nanocolloid injected around the tumour or the biopsy/tumour site (peritumoural, subdermal or periareolar for breast; intradermal around the melanoma/scar).
Dual localisation: radiotracer plus intra-operative blue dye — using both raises the sentinel-node identification rate above either alone.
Timing: imaging from minutes up to a few hours after injection; protocols use same-day (short) or day-before injection, so surgery is timed to residual node activity.
Imaging: dynamic & static planar gamma-camera images, with SPECT/CT added to give anatomical localisation of nodes.
📷 Image placeholder — planar lymphoscintigram showing an injection-site “star” artefact and a focal hot sentinel node in the axilla.
3What the scan shows
Drainage pattern: a lymphatic channel leading from the injection site to one or more focal “hot spots” — the sentinel node(s).
Number & site: confirms how many sentinel nodes there are and in which basin (e.g. axillary vs internal mammary in breast; unpredictable basins in truncal melanoma).
Aberrant / unexpected nodes: in-transit, interval or contralateral nodes, or drainage to an unanticipated basin — these would be missed without mapping.
SPECT/CT pinpoints the node relative to anatomy, aiding a targeted surgical approach and reducing operative time.
Non-visualisation of any node→re-inject / delayed imaging; rely more on blue dye & probe at surgery
4Safety, radiation & precautions
Radiation: the effective dose is low — the small administered activity of ⁹⁹ᵐTc gives a minor exposure to patient and theatre staff, well within occupational limits.
Blue dye: transient blue skin/urine staining and, importantly, a small risk of anaphylaxis to patent blue dye — the team must be prepared to treat it.
Pregnancy/breastfeeding: pregnancy is a relative contraindication; breastfeeding may need temporary interruption per local protocol.
🚩 Patent blue dye can cause anaphylaxis — pre-warn the anaesthetist, watch for hypotension & the transient artefactual drop in pulse-oximetry (SpO₂) the dye causes.
🎓 A negative sentinel node lets a patient avoid axillary/regional clearance and its lymphoedema — that morbidity-sparing is the whole point of SLNB, so quote it in exams.
NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL__IR — Vascular:
Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA), with or without stenting, is the mainstay endovascular treatment for peripheral arterial disease (PAD). Under image guidance a balloon catheter is passed across an arterial stenosis or occlusion and inflated to restore luminal patency; a stent or drug-coated balloon is deployed selectively when the angioplasty result is inadequate. It is a minimally invasive alternative to surgical bypass, particularly suited to focal disease of the iliac and femoropopliteal segments.

1Indication & patient selection

PTA is offered for symptomatic disease that limits the patient or threatens the limb, after optimisation of risk factors and supervised exercise.

Lifestyle-limiting intermittent claudication refractory to conservative therapy (exercise, smoking cessation, statin, antiplatelet).
Critical limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI): rest pain, ulceration or gangrene (Fontaine III–IV / Rutherford 4–6).
Anatomically suitable lesion on prior duplex, CT or MR angiography.
Focal short iliac stenosis (TASC A)→Endovascular therapy first-line, high patency
Long diffuse aorto-iliac occlusion (TASC D)→Surgical bypass traditionally favoured

The TASC (Trans-Atlantic Inter-Society Consensus) classification grades lesions A–D by length, number and calcification: A/B favour endovascular treatment, D favours open surgery, and C is decided case-by-case, though improving devices increasingly extend endovascular options.

2Access & crossing the lesion

Ultrasound-guided arterial puncture is standard, followed by a guidewire and vascular sheath (Seldinger technique).

Common femoral artery is the usual access: retrograde (up-and-over for contralateral iliac/femoral disease) or antegrade (for ipsilateral femoropopliteal/infrapopliteal lesions).
Radial or brachial access is an alternative for aorto-iliac work or hostile groins.
A guidewire is negotiated across the stenosis under fluoroscopy, aided by a digital subtraction angiography (DSA) roadmap; a support catheter directs the wire.
Wire will not cross intraluminally→Subintimal angioplasty with re-entry into true lumen
📷 Image placeholder — DSA run of a superficial femoral artery showing a focal stenosis before and after balloon angioplasty.
3Balloon dilatation, stenting & completion run

An appropriately sized angioplasty balloon is tracked over the wire across the lesion and inflated to a set pressure for a timed dilatation, fracturing the plaque and stretching the vessel wall.

Plain balloon PTA is often sufficient for iliac and femoropopliteal lesions.
A stent is deployed for suboptimal result, flow-limiting dissection or elastic recoil: self-expanding stents in mobile/femoropopliteal segments, balloon-mounted stents where precise placement is needed (e.g. ostial iliac).
A drug-coated (paclitaxel) balloon may be used to reduce restenosis, particularly in the superficial femoral artery.

A completion angiographic run confirms brisk in-line flow, resolution of the stenosis and preserved distal runoff before the sheath is removed.

🎓 “Leave nothing behind” philosophy: plain or drug-coated balloon angioplasty is often preferred over stenting across the mobile femoropopliteal segment, reserving stents for bailout, because stents there are prone to fracture and in-stent restenosis.
4Peri-procedural care & surveillance

Pre-procedure: informed consent; commence/continue aspirin, often with clopidogrel loading for stenting (dual antiplatelet therapy); check coagulation (INR, platelets) and renal function (eGFR/creatinine). Screen for iodinated-contrast issues — hydration and minimising contrast volume in renal impairment, and reviewing metformin and prior contrast reactions.

Post-procedure: puncture-site care with bed rest and manual compression or a closure device, and monitoring for haematoma; continue dual antiplatelet therapy (typically for a defined period after stenting, then lifelong single agent). Surveillance is by clinical review, ankle-brachial pressure index and duplex ultrasound to detect restenosis.

🩸Access-site haematoma / pseudoaneurysm
Commonest complication; US-guided compression or thrombin injection for pseudoaneurysm.
↕️Dissection
Flow-limiting flap treated by prolonged balloon inflation or stenting.
⚠️Distal embolisation
Debris showers runoff vessels; managed by aspiration or thrombolysis.
💥Vessel rupture
Over-dilatation causes extravasation; treated by balloon tamponade or covered stent.
🧪Contrast nephropathy
Mitigated by hydration and limiting iodinated contrast dose.
🔁Restenosis
Neointimal hyperplasia; detected on surveillance, may need reintervention.
🚩 Sudden severe procedural pain, hypotension or contrast extravasation on the completion run signals vessel rupture — keep the wire across, inflate a balloon to tamponade the site, and prepare a covered stent while summoning help.

Transcatheter arterial embolisation (TAE) is the endovascular control of acute haemorrhage: a catheter is steered from a peripheral artery to the bleeding vessel under digital subtraction angiography (DSA), and an embolic agent is deployed to occlude flow. It is a first-line or rescue haemostatic option across many territories — GI bleeding after failed or unavailable endoscopy, post-partum haemorrhage, solid-organ and pelvic trauma, intractable epistaxis, haemoptysis, and ruptured visceral aneurysms — and is performed with resuscitation running in parallel.

1Indications & parallel resuscitation
GI bleed — upper GI after failed/unavailable endoscopy; lower GI (diverticular, angiodysplasia) not reachable endoscopically.
Trauma — solid-organ injury (splenic, hepatic) or pelvic arterial bleeding in the haemodynamically stabilisable patient.
Obstetric — post-partum haemorrhage refractory to uterotonics/tamponade (uterine artery embolisation).
Others — intractable epistaxis (sphenopalatine/internal maxillary), haemoptysis (bronchial artery), ruptured visceral/splenic/hepatic aneurysm.
Ongoing transfusion requirement + bleeding source localised on CT angiography→Activate IR for emergency embolisation

Resuscitation does not wait for the angiography suite: large-bore access, blood products via major haemorrhage protocol, correct coagulopathy, and cross-match run concurrently. Consent (including risk of non-target embolisation and organ infarction) is taken where the patient is able.

2Access & selective angiography
Access — common femoral (or radial) artery puncture under ultrasound, Seldinger technique, sheath placed.
Roadmap — parent vessel catheterised, DSA run performed to identify the culprit and its collateral supply.
Superselective — a coaxial microcatheter is advanced distally into the feeding vessel to spare adjacent tissue.
Focal contrast extravasation / blush on DSA→Confirms active bleeding — this is the target to embolise
📷 Image placeholder — DSA showing focal contrast extravasation from a branch vessel before coil deployment.
3Choosing & deploying the embolic agent
🌀Coils
Permanent, precise mechanical occlusion of a named vessel; ideal for a discrete bleeding point or aneurysm neck.
🧽Gelfoam
Temporary gelatin sponge, resorbs over days; recanalisation allows tissue recovery — used in trauma/PPH.
⚪Particles (PVA / microspheres)
Distal small-vessel occlusion; effective for diffuse bleeds (e.g. bronchial artery, PPH) but higher ischaemia risk.
🧪Glue / Onyx
Liquid embolics that polymerise in the vessel; useful in coagulopathy and high-flow lesions, operator-dependent.
🩹Covered stent
Excludes the bleeding point while preserving flow — for large/end-arteries where occlusion would infarct (e.g. iliac, hepatic).

Proximal vs distal: proximal embolisation (e.g. splenic artery coiling) reduces perfusion pressure while collaterals preserve the organ; distal/superselective embolisation targets the exact bleeding segment but risks focal infarction. Empirical (blind) embolisation is deploying agent into the territory shown as the culprit on CT even when no active blush is seen at DSA — commonly used in localised GI bleeds and the sphenopalatine artery in epistaxis.

4Complications & post-procedure care
Non-target embolisation — agent lodges in the wrong territory (e.g. bowel, limb, spinal artery in bronchial embolisation causing paraplegia); minimised by superselective catheterisation and controlled injection.
End-organ ischaemia / infarction & necrosis — especially with distal particle embolisation or end-arteries; balanced against the fatal risk of ongoing bleeding.
Post-embolisation syndrome — self-limiting pain, low-grade fever, nausea and raised inflammatory markers over days; managed with analgesia and supportive care.
Access complications — groin haematoma, pseudoaneurysm, arterial dissection, contrast nephropathy.
🚩 Rebleeding after apparently successful embolisation demands repeat DSA — ongoing transfusion requirement, falling Hb, or return of haemodynamic instability should trigger re-look rather than watchful waiting.
🎓 On DSA, active contrast extravasation (a blush that persists into the venous phase) is the angiographic hallmark of active bleeding and the target for embolisation; its absence does not exclude intermittent bleeding, which is why empirical embolisation of the CT-identified culprit vessel is a valid strategy.

Uterine artery embolisation (UAE) is a minimally-invasive, uterine-sparing treatment for symptomatic uterine fibroids. By occluding the arterial supply to the fibroids, it induces infarction and shrinkage while preserving the uterus, offering an alternative for women who wish to avoid or defer hysterectomy or myomectomy. It is also a key emergency tool in intractable post-partum haemorrhage and has a growing role in symptomatic adenomyosis.

1Indications & patient selection

Offered for symptomatic fibroids causing menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding, anaemia) or bulk/pressure symptoms (pelvic pain, urinary frequency, abdominal distension) in women who wish to preserve the uterus or avoid surgery.

Menorrhagia with iron-deficiency anaemia refractory to medical therapy
Bulk symptoms: pressure, urinary frequency, mass effect
Emergency: intractable post-partum haemorrhage after failed medical/uterotonic measures
Symptomatic adenomyosis (uterine-sparing option)
Woman with symptomatic fibroids who actively desires future fertility→Myomectomy generally preferred; UAE may reduce ovarian reserve & fertility
2Pre-procedure work-up

Confirm fibroids and map their size, number and location on pelvic MRI (gold standard) or ultrasound. MRI also assesses vascularity and helps exclude leiomyosarcoma. Malignancy must be excluded and the endometrium assessed before proceeding.

MRI/US to confirm fibroids & exclude malignancy (leiomyosarcoma)
Detailed fertility discussion & documented informed consent
FBC (anaemia), coagulation/INR & platelets, group & save
Renal function (U&Es/eGFR) & contrast allergy check before iodinated contrast
Robust analgesia plan arranged — often patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)
📷 Image placeholder — sagittal T2 pelvic MRI showing an enlarged fibroid uterus with a bulky intramural leiomyoma.
3Technique & angiographic findings

Under fluoroscopic guidance, arterial access is gained (commonly common femoral, increasingly radial). A catheter is advanced over the aortic bifurcation and each internal iliac is engaged to selectively catheterise both uterine arteries. Embolic particles — polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) or calibrated microspheres — are injected to occlude the fibroid supply, producing infarction while the myometrium is spared by collateral flow.

Hypertrophied, tortuous, enlarged uterine arteries
Fibroid "blush" — hypervascular tumour staining on angiography
Endpoint: near-stasis / pruned vessels with loss of fibroid blush
Bilateral treatment essential — collateral supply causes failure if one side missed
Persistent fibroid blush from an ovarian artery collateral→Risk of incomplete treatment & non-target ovarian embolisation — assess carefully
4Complications & post-procedure care

Post-embolisation syndrome is expected in the first days: crampy pelvic pain, low-grade fever, nausea and malaise — managed with strong analgesia (often PCA), antiemetics and NSAIDs, not antibiotics. Watch for the true complications below.

🤒Post-embolisation syndrome
Pain, low-grade fever, malaise, nausea — expected, self-limiting, treated supportively
🩸Fibroid expulsion
Infarcted submucosal fibroid sloughs & is passed vaginally as discharge/tissue
🦠Infection / endometritis
Pyometra or sepsis — high, persistent fever & offensive discharge; needs antibiotics ± surgery
🥚Ovarian failure
Non-target embolisation of ovarian supply → reduced reserve, premature menopause, ↓ fertility
🎯Non-target embolisation
Particle reflux to bladder, buttock or ovary causing ischaemic injury
🩹Access-site injury
Groin haematoma, pseudoaneurysm or vessel dissection at the puncture site
🚩 Sustained high fever, worsening pain and offensive vaginal discharge days after UAE suggests endometritis/pyometra or septic fibroid degeneration — this is distinct from expected post-embolisation syndrome and mandates urgent antibiotics and gynaecology review.
🎓 If a woman wants to preserve fertility, myomectomy is generally preferred over UAE because embolisation carries a risk of diminished ovarian reserve and reduced fertility. UAE shines as a uterine-sparing option when fertility is not desired and in emergency post-partum haemorrhage.

Transarterial therapies exploit a key vascular quirk of the liver: normal hepatic parenchyma draws roughly three-quarters of its blood from the portal vein, whereas malignant nodules (hepatocellular carcinoma, HCC, and hypervascular metastases) are supplied almost entirely by the hepatic artery. Catheterising the artery that feeds the tumour therefore lets the interventional radiologist deliver a high local dose of chemotherapy, embolic particles, or radioactive microspheres directly to the tumour while largely sparing the surrounding liver. The two workhorse techniques are TACE (transarterial chemoembolisation) and TARE / SIRT (transarterial radioembolisation with Yttrium-90).

💉cTACE
Conventional TACE: chemotherapy (e.g. doxorubicin) emulsified in Lipiodol, then embolic particles → cytotoxic plus ischaemic kill.
🔵DEB-TACE
Drug-eluting beads pre-loaded with chemotherapy give sustained local drug release with lower systemic peaks.
☢️TARE / Y-90
Yttrium-90 glass or resin microspheres deliver internal beta radiation; minimally embolic ("radiation lobectomy").
🎯BCLC B target
Intermediate-stage HCC (multinodular, preserved liver function, no vascular invasion) is the classic TACE indication.
1Indications & patient selection
Intermediate-stage HCC (BCLC B) not amenable to resection, transplant or ablation → TACE is first-line.
HCC with segmental portal vein invasion or as a bridge/downstaging tool to transplant → TARE is often preferred.
Unresectable liver-dominant metastases (colorectal, neuroendocrine, ocular melanoma) → TARE or TACE.
Requires adequate liver reserve: Child-Pugh A (or well-compensated B), ECOG 0–1, and a bilirubin that is not markedly elevated.
Multinodular HCC, preserved function, no extrahepatic spread→BCLC B → TACE
2Pre-procedure work-up & consent
Cross-sectional imaging (triple-phase CT / MRI) to confirm arterial hypervascularity and map the tumour-feeding vessels.
Bloods: FBC, coagulation (INR / platelets), U&Es, LFTs, and tumour markers (AFP for HCC).
Correct coagulopathy: aim INR ≤ 1.5 and platelets ≥ 50 × 10⁹/L; withhold anticoagulants per protocol.
Fasting from ~6 hours before; IV access, antiemetics and analgesia prepared; antibiotic prophylaxis if biliary anatomy is altered (e.g. prior sphincterotomy).
TARE only: a separate mapping angiogram with 99mTc-MAA to measure the lung shunt fraction and exclude GI non-target flow, plus prophylactic coil embolisation of aberrant vessels.
🚩 A high lung shunt fraction on the Y-90 MAA work-up risks radiation pneumonitis and may reduce the deliverable dose or contraindicate treatment. Any uncorrectable gastroduodenal non-target deposition risks GI ulceration.
📷 Image placeholder — selective hepatic arteriogram showing a hypervascular tumour blush being catheterised via a microcatheter before embolisation.
3Technique
Access: ultrasound-guided common femoral (or radial) artery puncture, Seldinger technique, under local anaesthesia and fluoroscopic guidance.
Catheterisation: the coeliac axis and superior mesenteric artery are catheterised; a microcatheter is advanced superselectively into the segmental/subsegmental tumour-feeding artery.
Delivery — TACE: the chemotherapy–Lipiodol emulsion or drug-eluting beads are injected until arterial stasis, adding an embolic agent for the ischaemic hit.
Delivery — TARE: the prescribed activity of Y-90 microspheres is infused; being minimally embolic, flow is largely preserved and the kill is radiobiological.
Completion angiography confirms devascularisation/target coverage; the sheath is removed and haemostasis achieved with manual pressure or a closure device.
4Complications, contraindications & aftercare
🤒Post-embolisation syndrome
Commonest sequela: fever, RUQ pain, nausea, malaise; self-limiting over days, managed supportively.
🫀Liver decompensation
Ischaemic/radiation insult can precipitate liver failure, ascites or jaundice, especially with poor reserve.
⚠️Non-target injury
Reflux of agent → GI ulceration, cholecystitis, pancreatitis; Y-90 lung shunting → radiation pneumonitis.
🧫Biliary / infective
Biliary injury, bilomas, abscess formation, and access-site bleeding or arterial dissection.
Contraindications: Child-Pugh C / poor liver reserve, main portal vein thrombosis (a relative/caution for TACE due to ischaemia risk), uncorrectable coagulopathy, and large-volume extrahepatic disease.
Aftercare: monitor observations and the puncture site, IV fluids, analgesia and antiemetics, watch for post-embolisation syndrome, and repeat imaging (typically at ~4–6 weeks / mRECIST) to assess response.
🎓 Portal vein status is the classic exam discriminator: main portal vein thrombosis favours TARE over TACE, because Y-90 is minimally embolic and less likely to tip a compromised liver into ischaemic failure.

Catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) and thrombectomy are image-guided techniques for removing or dissolving acute thrombus. A multi-side-hole catheter is advanced into the clot under fluoroscopy and a thrombolytic agent (e.g. alteplase/tPA) is infused directly into the thrombus, typically over several hours with repeat venography. Mechanical adjuncts (pharmacomechanical or aspiration thrombectomy devices) may be added to speed clot clearance and reduce lytic dose. The unifying principle is delivering therapy at the clot interface to restore flow while limiting systemic drug exposure.

1Indications & patient selection
Acute limb ischaemia — thrombosed bypass graft or native artery, where the limb is viable but threatened.
Extensive iliofemoral DVT — to reduce post-thrombotic syndrome in selected younger patients with good functional status and low bleeding risk.
Massive / submassive PE — catheter-directed therapy for haemodynamic compromise or right-heart strain.
Large-vessel-occlusion stroke — mechanical thrombectomy is the interventional-neuroradiology equivalent for acute ischaemic stroke.
Acutely cold, painful, pulseless leg with a known femoropopliteal graft→Consider catheter-directed thrombolysis of the occluded graft
2Pre-procedure work-up
Check coagulation (INR / APTT), platelets and baseline fibrinogen before starting lysis.
Actively exclude contraindications to thrombolysis — recent surgery, active bleeding, recent stroke or intracranial pathology, recent GI bleed, uncontrolled hypertension.
Obtain informed consent covering the major risk of haemorrhage, and confirm renal function for iodinated contrast.
Set up monitoring: serial fibrinogen during the infusion (stop or reduce lysis if fibrinogen falls markedly, e.g. <1 g/L), plus neuro and puncture-site observations.
🚩 Absolute contraindications to lysis include active internal bleeding, recent haemorrhagic or ischaemic stroke, recent major surgery/trauma, and intracranial neoplasm or vascular malformation — screen for these before every case.
3Technique
Access — ultrasound-guided vascular puncture (e.g. popliteal, femoral or jugular depending on target), then fluoroscopic guidance.
Cross the clot — a guidewire and catheter are manipulated through the thrombus; diagnostic venography/angiography defines its extent.
Position infusion catheter — a multi-side-hole catheter is embedded across the length of the thrombus so tPA is delivered throughout the clot.
Infuse & reassess — thrombolytic infused over hours; patient returns to the angio suite for repeat venography to check progress, ± pharmacomechanical or aspiration thrombectomy and treatment of any unmasked underlying stenosis (angioplasty/stent).
📷 Image placeholder — fluoroscopic run showing a multi-side-hole infusion catheter embedded within an occluded iliofemoral segment, with contrast opacifying the thrombus.
4Complications & mitigation
🩸Major bleeding / ICH
The key risk; intracranial haemorrhage is the feared catastrophe. Mitigate with strict patient selection, fibrinogen monitoring and prompt cessation.
🧩Distal embolisation
Fragmented clot showers downstream, worsening ischaemia; may need aspiration or continued lysis.
⚡Reperfusion injury
Restored flow to ischaemic muscle can cause compartment syndrome and hyperkalaemia; watch limb pressures.
☢️Contrast issues
Contrast-induced nephropathy and allergy; hydrate and check renal function beforehand.
🎓 Mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel-occlusion ischaemic stroke is performed by interventional neuroradiology and is the CNS equivalent of the peripheral techniques described here — same principle of catheter-based clot removal, different territory.

Gonadal (testicular/ovarian) vein embolisation is a percutaneous, catheter-based interventional-radiology procedure that occludes an incompetent gonadal vein. In men it treats a symptomatic varicocele; in women it treats pelvic congestion syndrome. Both share the same underlying problem — venous reflux down a valveless or incompetent gonadal vein — and the same fix: catheterise the vein, confirm reflux on venography, then occlude it with coils ± sclerosant.

♂️Varicocele
Dilated pampiniform plexus; usually LEFT-sided; causes ache, subfertility with impaired semen parameters.
♀️Pelvic congestion
Chronic pelvic pain + vulvar/pelvic varices in multiparous women; female equivalent via ovarian vein.
🧵Coils ± sclerosant
Embolic agents that occlude the refluxing vein along its length.
🩻Fluoroscopy
Real-time guidance for catheter navigation, venography and controlled coil deployment.
1Indication & work-up
Symptomatic varicocele: dragging scrotal ache, palpable “bag of worms”, or subfertility with impaired semen parameters.
Left-sided predominance: the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein at a near right angle, raising venous pressure and promoting reflux.
Female equivalent: pelvic congestion syndrome — chronic pelvic pain, worse on standing, with vulvar/pelvic varices in multiparous women.
New right-sided varicocele that does NOT decompress when lying flat→Image the retroperitoneum — exclude a renal/retroperitoneal mass obstructing venous drainage.
Work-up: scrotal/pelvic Doppler ultrasound to confirm reflux and grade the varicocele; semen analysis where subfertility is the driver; informed consent covering benefits, risks and the alternative of surgical ligation.
2Access & catheterisation
Venous access is obtained under ultrasound guidance, usually via the right internal jugular vein or the common femoral vein. A catheter is advanced into the left renal vein and then selectively into the gonadal (testicular/ovarian) vein. Procedure is performed under local anaesthetic with the patient awake.
📷 Image placeholder — venogram of a refluxing left gonadal vein with catheter in situ and coils being deployed.
3Venography & embolisation
Venography confirms reflux down the gonadal vein and maps any collateral or duplicated channels that could cause recurrence.
The vein is occluded with coils, often combined with a sclerosant (e.g. sodium tetradecyl sulphate) to close small collaterals.
Occlusion typically extends along the length of the vein down to the level of reflux, not just a single point.
Completion venography confirms cessation of reflux before catheter removal.
4Advantages, complications & aftercare
Advantages over surgical ligation: no general anaesthetic, day-case procedure, faster recovery and quick return to normal activity.
➡️Coil migration
Coil dislodges to the renal vein/pulmonary circulation; mitigated by correct sizing and controlled deployment.
🎯Non-target embolisation
Sclerosant/coil reaching unintended vessels; minimised with careful venographic control.
🩸Vein perforation
Gonadal vein injury during catheterisation; usually self-limiting but can cause pain/extravasation.
🔁Recurrence
Persistent reflux via missed collaterals; reduced by embolising the full length of the vein.
Other risks: contrast reaction and radiation exposure. Gonadal radiation dose is relevant in young men but is generally low and considered acceptable. Aftercare: short observation, simple analgesia, and follow-up Doppler and/or semen analysis to confirm success.
Sudden pleuritic chest pain or breathlessness after coil deployment→Suspect coil migration to the pulmonary circulation — imaging and retrieval may be needed.
🚩 A NEW right-sided or non-decompressing varicocele in an older man is a red flag — it may signal renal cell carcinoma with tumour thrombus or retroperitoneal obstruction of gonadal venous drainage, and warrants cross-sectional imaging before any embolisation.
🎓 Left-sided predominance is the classic exam point: the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle (higher pressure, longer column), whereas the right gonadal vein drains obliquely straight into the IVC. Embolisation avoids general anaesthetic and offers faster recovery than open/laparoscopic ligation.

An inferior vena cava (IVC) filter is a metallic cage deployed percutaneously into the IVC to mechanically trap thromboemboli arising from lower-limb and pelvic deep vein thrombosis (DVT), preventing them from reaching the pulmonary arteries. It does not treat the clot or replace anticoagulation — it is a purely mechanical barrier used when anticoagulation cannot be given or has failed. Most modern filters are retrievable, and a clear plan for removal is part of the procedure from the outset.

1Confirm the indication & consent

The core indication is venous thromboembolism (VTE) where anticoagulation is unsafe or ineffective. Document the specific reason clearly in the notes.

Proven DVT/PE with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation (e.g. active major haemorrhage, recent intracranial bleed, immediate major surgery).
Recurrent PE despite adequate, therapeutic anticoagulation.
Selected prophylaxis in very high-risk patients (major trauma, some peri-operative cases) — more controversial.
Large proximal DVT + active GI bleed, cannot anticoagulate→Retrievable IVC filter to cover the high-risk period

Consent covers the risks below and, crucially, the plan and timeframe for retrieval. Check coagulation status (INR, platelets); coagulopathy is corrected as feasible, but access is possible even in bleeding patients since the filter itself addresses the VTE risk.

2Venous access & cavography

Ultrasound-guided venous puncture is obtained via the right internal jugular or common femoral vein, and a sheath is advanced into the IVC over a guidewire under fluoroscopy.

Cavography (contrast venogram) maps the IVC and confirms it is patent and free of thrombus at the intended deployment site.
Measure the IVC diameter — most filters are certified up to ~28–30 mm; a megacava may need a different device or bilateral iliac filters.
Identify the renal vein ostia — the landmark that determines deployment level.
📷 Image placeholder — cavogram showing the IVC, renal vein inflow, and a deployed infrarenal filter under fluoroscopy.
3Deploy in the infrarenal IVC

The filter is positioned so its apex sits just below the lowest renal vein and deployed under fluoroscopic guidance in the infrarenal IVC.

Infrarenal placement means that if the filter thromboses, renal venous drainage is preserved above the clot.
A suprarenal position is reserved for special cases (e.g. renal vein or gonadal-vein thrombus, pregnancy, thrombus extending above the renal veins).
A completion cavogram confirms satisfactory position and full expansion, and the sheath is removed with haemostasis at the access site.
4Plan retrieval & follow-up

Retrievable filters should be removed once anticoagulation can be safely started or the transient high-risk period has passed. The longer a filter dwells, the higher the rate of complications and the harder retrieval becomes as it endothelialises.

GI bleed resolved, patient can now be anticoagulated→Start anticoagulation and retrieve the filter
🚩 Retained retrievable filters are a recognised patient-safety problem — every filter needs a documented tracking and retrieval plan so it is not simply forgotten. Unretrieved filters accumulate risk of tilt, penetration, fracture and IVC occlusion.
🎓 An IVC filter prevents PE but does NOT treat the DVT or lower the clot burden — anticoagulation should be (re)started as soon as it is safe, and the filter retrieved thereafter.
➡️Migration
Filter shifts cranially or caudally, occasionally to the heart or pulmonary artery.
📌Penetration
Struts perforate the IVC wall, sometimes into the aorta, duodenum or ureter.
🩸Filter thrombosis
Trapped clot occludes the filter/IVC, causing lower-limb swelling and IVC occlusion.
⚙️Fracture
Strut fracture with embolisation of fragments, a risk that rises with dwell time.
🔁Recurrent DVT
Filters reduce PE but increase the rate of recurrent lower-limb DVT.
🪝Failed retrieval
Tilt or endothelialisation makes the filter irretrievable, leaving it permanent.

Image-guided central venous access places long-term catheters with the tip at the cavoatrial junction under ultrasound and fluoroscopic guidance. Choosing the right device — PICC, tunnelled cuffed line, or implantable port — depends on the indication, expected duration of therapy, and infection risk.

💉PICC
Peripherally inserted via basilic/brachial vein, tip at cavoatrial junction. Medium-term (weeks–months) IV antibiotics, chemo, TPN. Easy to place/remove; higher thrombosis risk in-arm.
🧵Tunnelled cuffed (Hickman/Groshong)
Subcutaneous tunnel + Dacron cuff that promotes fibrosis to anchor the line and act as an infection barrier. For chemo, TPN, apheresis. Externally accessible lumens.
🔘Implantable port
Totally subcutaneous reservoir accessed transcutaneously by a non-coring (Huber) needle. Best for intermittent long-term chemo — lowest infection rate, best cosmesis.
⏱️Non-tunnelled line
Directly through skin into a central vein for short-term use (days) — inpatient access, ICU, dialysis bridging. Highest infection risk if left in situ.
1Indication & device selection

Confirm the indication and the expected duration of therapy — this drives the choice of device. Match need to risk profile.

Medium-term IV antibiotics / chemo → PICC
Prolonged continuous chemo, TPN, apheresis → tunnelled cuffed line
Intermittent long-term chemo, best cosmesis → implantable port
Short-term inpatient access only → non-tunnelled line
Intermittent chemo over many months, lowest infection risk wanted→Implantable port
2Pre-procedure checks
Written informed consent; confirm indication and expected duration
Coagulation screen: platelets ≥ 50 × 10⁹/L, INR ≤ 1.5 (correct if outside range)
Review anticoagulants/antiplatelets and hold per local protocol
Aseptic technique; prophylactic antibiotics not routinely required for routine insertion
3Technique — US puncture & fluoroscopic tip placement

The right internal jugular vein is a common access route for tunnelled lines and ports because it gives a direct, low-thrombosis path to the SVC. PICCs use the basilic or brachial vein at the mid-upper arm.

Real-time ultrasound-guided venous puncture — reduces arterial puncture and pneumothorax
Seldinger technique: guidewire, peel-away sheath, catheter railroaded over wire
Tunnelled devices: create a subcutaneous tunnel, seat the Dacron cuff a few cm from the exit site
Fluoroscopic confirmation that guidewire and catheter tip sit at the cavoatrial junction
📷 Image placeholder — fluoroscopic spot image showing a right IJ tunnelled catheter with tip at the cavoatrial junction.
4Complications & post-procedure care
🫁Pneumothorax
Pleural puncture during subclavian/low IJ access; US guidance lowers risk. Check CXR post-procedure.
🩸Arterial puncture
Inadvertent carotid/subclavian artery entry — risk of haematoma; avoided by real-time US.
💨Air embolism
Air entrained through open sheath; mitigated by Trendelenburg and Valsalva during exchange.
📍Malposition / tip migration
Tip too high, in azygos or up IJ; confirmed and corrected under fluoroscopy.
🦠CRBSI
Catheter-related bloodstream infection — lowest with ports, highest with non-tunnelled lines.
🧊Thrombosis
Catheter-associated venous thrombosis, more common with arm PICCs and small-vein/large-catheter mismatch.
Sudden pleuritic chest pain / breathlessness after insertion→Suspect pneumothorax — urgent CXR
🚩 A post-procedure CXR is mandatory after neck/chest central access to confirm the tip at the cavoatrial junction and to exclude a pneumothorax before the line is used.
🎓 The correct tip position is the cavoatrial junction: too high (upper SVC) risks thrombosis and fibrin sheath; too low (right atrium) risks arrhythmia and myocardial perforation.

Image-guided percutaneous drainage is the first-line management for most accessible fluid collections and abscesses, offering a minimally invasive alternative to surgery. Under real-time ultrasound or CT guidance, a catheter is placed into the collection to evacuate infected or symptomatic fluid, allowing source control while the patient is stabilised and cross-sectional anatomy is respected. It is performed by interventional radiology after review of the diagnostic imaging, coagulation status and antibiotic cover.

1Indications & pre-procedure work-up

Drainage is indicated for symptomatic or infected collections where percutaneous access is safe: intra-abdominal or pelvic abscess (e.g. post-appendicectomy, diverticular, tubo-ovarian), empyema, infected pancreatic/peripancreatic collection, and pyogenic liver abscess. It is preferred over open surgery for any collection with a safe access window.

Review cross-sectional imaging (CT/US/MRI) to size the collection, confirm it is drainable and plan a route avoiding bowel, vessels and pleura.
Check coagulation: aim INR ≤ 1.5 and platelets ≥ 50 × 10⁹/L; correct or hold anticoagulants/antiplatelets per protocol.
Give peri-procedural antibiotics, obtain informed consent, and secure IV access & monitoring; fast if sedation is planned.
Deep pelvic collection, no safe anterior route→Consider transgluteal, transvaginal or transrectal access
2Guidance & access route

Ultrasound gives real-time needle visualisation and no ionising radiation, ideal for superficial or clearly visible collections (liver, pleural, superficial pelvic). CT is used for deep, small or anatomically difficult collections (retroperitoneal, deep pelvic, pancreatic) where a precise trajectory around bowel and vessels is essential. The key principle is choosing the shortest safe window that avoids bowel loops, major vessels, solid organ hila and the pleural reflection.

📷 Image placeholder — CT-guided placement of a pigtail catheter into a rim-enhancing intra-abdominal collection.
3Technique: aspiration vs catheter drainage

Under aseptic technique and local anaesthetic, access is gained by one of two methods:

Seldinger: fine needle into the collection → guidewire passed → serial dilatation of the tract → locking pigtail catheter railroaded over the wire. Preferred for deeper or more difficult collections.
Trocar: catheter mounted on a stiffening trocar advanced directly into a large superficial collection in a single pass.

Aspirate a sample and send for microscopy, culture & sensitivity (MC&S). A diagnostic aspiration alone may suffice for a small collection, whereas a larger or frankly purulent collection warrants a catheter left in situ. The catheter is secured, connected to a gravity bag or low-pressure suction, and the initial drained volume documented.

🩸Bleeding
Vessel or solid-organ injury along the tract; mitigated by correcting coagulopathy and avoiding vascular structures.
🦠Sepsis / bacteraemia
Manipulation seeds organisms into the blood; give antibiotics and avoid over-vigorous irrigation.
🕳️Bowel / organ injury
Transgression of a bowel loop; avoided by careful trajectory planning on cross-sectional imaging.
🚱Catheter blockage
Thick or loculated pus occludes the lumen; prevented by regular saline flushing and adequate bore.
🔗Dislodgement
Catheter pulls out; a locking-loop pigtail and secure fixation reduce the risk.
🌀Fistula
Enteric or biliary communication may develop and delay resolution.
4Post-procedure care, loculation & removal

Nurse the catheter to gravity or suction; flush regularly (e.g. 10 mL saline) to maintain patency and chart daily output. A multiloculated collection may not drain through one catheter and can need multiple drains or intracavitary fibrinolytics. For empyema, intrapleural tPA plus DNase breaks down septations and reduces viscosity, improving drainage and often avoiding surgery.

Monitor clinical response: falling temperature, inflammatory markers and drain output signal success.
Obtain follow-up imaging (US/CT) to confirm the collection has collapsed and the catheter is well positioned.
Remove the catheter when output is < 10–20 mL/day, the patient is improving and imaging shows resolution.
Persistently high output with feculent fluid→Suspect an enteric fistula — tube study / cross-sectional imaging
🚩 New haemodynamic instability, brisk bleeding or worsening sepsis during or after drainage demands urgent resuscitation, senior review and repeat imaging — consider vascular injury, bowel perforation or seeding bacteraemia.
🎓 Percutaneous drainage is first-line over surgery for accessible collections; always send aspirate for MC&S, and remember intrapleural tPA/DNase as the medical adjunct for loculated empyema.

Percutaneous nephrostomy (PCN) is an image-guided procedure in which a catheter is placed directly through the flank into the renal collecting system to relieve obstruction and drain urine. It is one of the commonest emergency interventional-radiology procedures: the classic indication is an obstructed, infected system (pyonephrosis), a true urological emergency requiring urgent decompression. Once access is established, an antegrade ureteric stent can be passed down the ureter into the bladder to internalise drainage.

1Indications

PCN is used to decompress an obstructed kidney or to gain access to the collecting system.

Infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis) — pus under pressure; urgent decompression is life-saving.
Relief of obstruction — malignant (e.g. pelvic tumour, retroperitoneal fibrosis), stone, or stricture, especially with deteriorating renal function or after failed retrograde stenting.
Urinary diversion — for a ureteric leak or fistula, to divert urine away from the injury.
Access — for antegrade ureteric stenting or percutaneous stone treatment (PCNL).
Obstructed kidney + fever/sepsis + hydronephrosis→Pyonephrosis — emergency PCN to decompress
🚩 An infected, obstructed kidney is a urological emergency. Antibiotics alone cannot clear pus behind an obstruction — urgent drainage (PCN or retrograde stent) is required to prevent overwhelming sepsis and irreversible renal loss.
2Pre-procedure requirements
Coagulation — check INR and platelets; correct coagulopathy. Typical targets INR ≤ 1.5 and platelets ≥ 50 × 10⁹/L. Review antiplatelets/anticoagulants.
Antibiotics — prophylactic (or therapeutic if infected) cover before puncture, as manipulation of an infected system releases bacteraemia.
Consent — explain bleeding, sepsis, injury to adjacent organs, tube dislodgement, and possible failure.
Imaging review — recent US/CT to confirm hydronephrosis, plan the calyx and safe access track, and avoid bowel/pleura.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the scan / procedural image: fluoroscopic nephrostogram showing contrast opacifying a dilated collecting system with a pigtail catheter looped in the renal pelvis.
3Technique

Performed under local anaesthetic (± sedation) using combined ultrasound and fluoroscopy guidance.

Position — prone or prone-oblique, affected side accessible.
Puncture — US-guided needle into a posterior lower-pole calyx; this line-of-Brödel avascular plane and lower-pole route minimise vascular and pleural injury.
Access — aspirate urine to confirm position, inject contrast (nephrostogram), then pass a guidewire and coil it in the collecting system.
Dilatation & catheter — dilate the track over the wire and deploy a self-retaining locking pigtail nephrostomy catheter, secured to the skin and connected to a drainage bag.
Antegrade stent — if internal drainage is needed, a guidewire is negotiated down the ureter across the obstruction into the bladder and a double-J ureteric stent deployed antegrade; a covering nephrostomy is often left on free drainage initially.
🎓 Always target a posterior lower-pole calyx: posterior calyces lie in the relatively avascular plane, and a lower-pole approach keeps you below the pleural reflection (12th rib), avoiding pneumothorax. An upper-pole puncture risks the pleura and lung.
4Complications & post-procedure care
🩸Bleeding / haematuria
Kidney is highly vascular; transient haematuria is common. Significant bleeding may form an AV fistula or pseudoaneurysm needing embolisation.
🦠Sepsis
Especially when draining an infected system. Mitigate with antibiotics and gentle, low-pressure technique — avoid over-distending an infected pelvis.
🫁Bowel / pleural injury
Colon can be traversed; upper-pole puncture risks pneumothorax or hydrothorax. Avoided by lower-pole access and image guidance.
🔌Tube dislodgement
Catheter can fall out or block. Secure well, flush as needed, and educate the patient; early dislodgement may require re-access.
Post-procedure — monitor observations for bleeding/sepsis, chart drain output, keep the catheter to a bag on free drainage, and flush per protocol.
Renal recovery — watch for a post-obstructive diuresis after decompression, replacing fluid and electrolytes.

Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (PTC) and biliary drainage (PTBD) provide image-guided access to the biliary tree through the liver, used chiefly to decompress an obstructed system when ERCP has failed or is not feasible. A fine needle punctures a peripheral bile duct, a cholangiogram maps the level and cause of obstruction, and a guidewire is manipulated across the stricture to place an external, internal-external, or fully internal (stented) drain.

1INDICATIONS & PATIENT SELECTION
Relief of biliary obstruction — malignant (cholangiocarcinoma, pancreatic head cancer, hilar Klatskin tumour, nodal compression) or benign stricture.
First-line drainage when ERCP has failed or is impossible — altered anatomy (Roux-en-Y, gastrectomy), high hilar strictures, or an inaccessible papilla.
Acute cholangitis needing urgent decompression of an infected, obstructed system.
Access route for stone removal, stricture dilatation, or stent insertion (plastic or SEMS).
Hilar Klatskin tumour or failed ERCP→Percutaneous transhepatic route preferred
2PRE-PROCEDURE PREPARATION
Correct coagulopathy — obstructive jaundice causes malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamin K, so check INR/platelets and give IV vitamin K ± FFP/platelets; typical thresholds INR ≤ 1.5 and platelets ≥ 50 × 10⁹/L.
Prophylactic broad-spectrum IV antibiotics — the obstructed biliary tree is frequently colonised and instrumentation causes bacteraemia.
Informed consent (bleeding, sepsis, bile leak, failure), fasting, IV access, and review of prior cross-sectional imaging to plan the level of obstruction and puncture side.
🚩 Uncorrected coagulopathy is the key modifiable risk — the transhepatic tract crosses vascular liver parenchyma, so bleeding and haemobilia are the feared early complications.
3TECHNIQUE & IMAGING GUIDANCE
Ultrasound ± fluoroscopy guides a fine (Chiba) needle into a dilated peripheral bile duct; a right mid-axillary or anterior subxiphoid (left duct) approach is used.
Contrast is injected under fluoroscopy for the diagnostic cholangiogram, defining the anatomy and the level of obstruction.
A guidewire is negotiated across the stricture into the duodenum; the tract is dilated and a drainage catheter placed — external (above the block), internal-external (side-holes above and below), or a self-expanding metal / plastic stent for internalisation and palliation.
Wire will not cross the stricture at first attempt→Leave an external drain, allow decompression, then re-attempt internalisation later
📷 Image placeholder — PTC cholangiogram showing dilated intrahepatic ducts and an abrupt hilar stricture with a drain across it.
4COMPLICATIONS & POST-PROCEDURE CARE
🩸Bleeding / haemobilia
Injury to hepatic artery or portal vein along the tract; may need embolisation.
🦠Sepsis / cholangitis
Bacteraemia from an infected system; cover with antibiotics, avoid over-injection.
💧Bile leak / peritonitis
Bile extravasation causing chemical bile peritonitis and pain.
🫁Pneumothorax
From an intercostal puncture above the pleural reflection.
🔧Tube problems
Blockage, dislodgement, or pericatheter leak needing exchange or flushing.
Post-procedure: monitor observations for bleeding and sepsis, keep external drains on free drainage initially, and record output.
A completion or delayed check cholangiogram confirms position before capping or internalising the drain.
🎓 In malignant hilar obstruction, draining as little as one lobe representing ≥ 30% of functioning liver volume can relieve jaundice — routine drainage of both lobes is not always required.

Radiologically-inserted gastrostomy (RIG) is the fluoroscopically-guided placement of a feeding tube directly through the anterior abdominal wall into the stomach, creating durable enteral access when oral intake is inadequate or unsafe. It is the radiological alternative to an endoscopic (PEG) or surgical gastrostomy, and is particularly valuable when an obstructing pharyngeal or oesophageal tumour prevents passage of an endoscope, or when a patient cannot safely tolerate sedation.

1Indication & MDT decision

RIG provides long-term enteral feeding where swallowing is inadequate or unsafe. The commonest referrals are head & neck cancer and neurological disease.

Head & neck cancer — an obstructing pharyngeal/oesophageal tumour blocks the endoscope, so a per-oral PEG is impossible; RIG bypasses the obstruction entirely.
Neurological dysphagia — stroke and motor neurone disease (MND) with unsafe swallow and aspiration risk.
MND with poor respiratory reserve — a low forced vital capacity (FVC) makes endoscopy/sedation hazardous; RIG needs no endoscope or deep sedation, so is often better tolerated.
Obstructing pharyngeal/oesophageal tumour — endoscope cannot pass→RIG rather than PEG

The decision is made by an MDT with dietitian/nutrition team input, confirming feeding is appropriate and consistent with the patient's overall goals of care.

2Pre-procedure preparation
Coagulation — check INR and platelets; correct coagulopathy and hold/bridge anticoagulants and antiplatelets per protocol (this is a category with bleeding risk).
Aspiration risk — patients are frequently high-risk; nurse head-up and minimise over-distension.
Fasting — nil by mouth (typically ≥6 hours) so the stomach is empty.
Antibiotics — prophylaxis to reduce peristomal infection.
Consent — explaining the alternatives (PEG, surgical) and the specific risks below.

A nasogastric (NG) tube is placed beforehand to allow the stomach to be insufflated on the table.

3Technique under fluoroscopy

The procedure is performed supine under fluoroscopic guidance, usually with local anaesthetic ± light sedation.

Insufflate — air or CO₂ is instilled via the NG tube to distend the stomach and bring it into apposition with the anterior abdominal wall.
Confirm a safe window — screen to ensure the distended stomach lies against the abdominal wall, clear of the transverse colon and the liver edge.
Gastropexy — T-fasteners (retention sutures) anchor the stomach to the abdominal wall, opposing it and reducing leak/peritonitis.
Seldinger puncture — needle puncture between the T-fasteners, pass a guidewire, dilate the tract, and place the gastrostomy tube over the wire; position confirmed with contrast.
📷 Image placeholder — fluoroscopic image of the air-distended stomach with T-fastener gastropexy and the gastrostomy tube in situ.
4RIG vs PEG vs surgical & complications
RIG (radiological) — fluoroscopic, no endoscope; ideal when a tumour obstructs the upper GI tract or endoscopy/sedation is unsafe (e.g. MND with low FVC).
PEG (endoscopic) — needs a patent oesophagus and the endoscope to transilluminate the abdominal wall; usually requires sedation.
Surgical gastrostomy — open/laparoscopic, reserved for when both RIG and PEG fail or are contraindicated, or during another operation.

Key complications to counsel for and monitor:

☢️Peritonitis / misplacement
Tube outside the stomach or intraperitoneal leak; new pain, fever, sepsis — gastropexy mitigates this.
☢️Bleeding
From the tract or gastric wall; minimised by correcting coagulopathy pre-procedure.
☢️Colonic / visceral injury
Puncture of interposed transverse colon or liver; avoided by confirming a clear window.
☢️Aspiration
From gastric distension/reflux in a high-risk patient; limit insufflation and nurse head-up.
☢️Peristomal infection / leak
Skin infection or gastric leak around the stoma; antibiotic prophylaxis and stoma care reduce risk.
☢️Blockage / dislodgement
Tube blocks or falls out; flush regularly and replace early to keep the tract open.
🚩 New abdominal pain, fever, tachycardia, or peritonism after a RIG suggests tube misplacement or intraperitoneal leak causing peritonitis — stop feed, obtain a contrast tube-check, and escalate urgently.
🎓 In MND, a low FVC (typically <50% predicted) makes PEG sedation hazardous — RIG is preferred because it avoids the endoscope and deep sedation, and gastrostomy is best placed before respiratory function deteriorates further.

Percutaneous endovascular retrieval is the removal of an intravascular foreign body from the venous or arterial system under fluoroscopic guidance, without open surgery. The commonest culprits are fractured or embolised catheter fragments — a sheared central line or PICC, a fractured port (Portacath) catheter — but also migrated coils or stents, guidewire fragments, and malpositioned or displaced devices. Retained intravascular foreign bodies are not benign: they risk thrombosis, sepsis, cardiac arrhythmia, valve/chamber perforation and pulmonary embolism, so retrieval is recommended even when the patient is asymptomatic. The workhorse tool is the loop snare, supplemented by forceps and basket devices.

🧵Sheared CVC / PICC fragment
Pinch-off or catheter fracture; fragment embolises to SVC, right atrium or pulmonary artery. Most common retrieval target.
💉Port catheter fracture
Portacath tubing fractures at the clavicle-first-rib ‘pinch-off’ point and migrates centrally.
🌀Migrated coil / stent
Embolisation coil or vascular stent displaced from its intended site during or after deployment.
🪝Guidewire fragment
Retained or sheared guidewire, often iatrogenic during line insertion; may lodge in the great veins or right heart.
🕸️Displaced / migrated IVC filter
Malpositioned or migrated inferior vena cava filter requiring repositioning or retrieval.
1Pre-procedure: localise, consent, coagulation
Confirm and localise the fragment on imaging (chest radiograph ± CT / fluoroscopy) — note position, orientation and whether a free end is available to snare.
Informed consent covering vascular/cardiac injury, arrhythmia, failure to retrieve and further migration, and the possibility of surgical backup.
Check coagulation: correct significant coagulopathy, aim INR ≤ 1.5 and platelets ≥ 50 × 10⁹/L; review anticoagulants/antiplatelets.
IV access, monitoring (ECG, SpO₂, BP) and local anaesthetic; most cases need no general anaesthetic.
Free end of fragment visible in the lumen→Ideal for a loop snare — grab the free end and withdraw
2Access and fluoroscopic localisation
Ultrasound-guided venous puncture, usually the right common femoral vein (large calibre, straight route to the SVC/right heart); internal jugular access is an alternative.
Place a vascular sheath — sized generously to allow the captured fragment to be withdrawn without stripping it off at the sheath tip.
Advance under fluoroscopy and confirm the fragment’s position; a diagnostic catheter can be used to reposition a fragment with no free end so an end becomes graspable.
📷 Image placeholder — fluoroscopic image of a gooseneck loop snare capturing an embolised catheter fragment in the right atrium.
3Capture and withdrawal
Loop snare (workhorse): a gooseneck snare loop is passed over the free end, the loop tightened to grip, and the fragment drawn back to and through the sheath.
Forceps / basket: used when no free end is snareable, to grasp awkwardly orientated or wedged fragments.
Manipulate gently near the heart to minimise arrhythmia; remove the fragment, sheath and any device as a unit, then confirm complete retrieval.
🎓 The loop (gooseneck) snare is the first-line retrieval device and works best when a free end of the foreign body lies free within the vessel lumen — a favourite single-best-answer fact.
4Complications and post-procedure care
Vascular or cardiac injury / perforation and tamponade during manipulation near the heart.
Arrhythmia provoked by wire/catheter contact with the right heart — continuous ECG monitoring throughout.
Fragment loss or further migration (e.g. to a distal pulmonary artery), and access-site complications (haematoma, thrombosis, infection).
Post-procedure: manual compression / haemostasis at the puncture site, observation with vital-sign monitoring, and imaging to confirm the foreign body is gone.
🚩 New hypotension, tachycardia or a rising JVP during or after right-heart manipulation suggests cardiac perforation and tamponade — stop, image (echo) urgently and escalate to cardiothoracic surgery.

Image-guided percutaneous biopsy uses real-time or cross-sectional imaging to advance a needle into a target lesion and retrieve tissue for histology or cytology. It is the workhorse diagnostic procedure of interventional radiology, allowing a lung nodule, liver or renal mass, lymph node, bone or soft-tissue lesion to be characterised, a malignancy typed and staged, or infected tissue sampled for microbiology — all without open surgery.

1Indications & sample type: FNA vs core

Biopsy is requested to obtain a tissue diagnosis when imaging alone cannot characterise a lesion, to confirm and type a suspected malignancy, to stage disease (e.g. sampling a distant node), or to identify an organism in suspected infection.

Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) — fine needle (e.g. 22–25G), yields cells for cytology. Good for confirming metastatic nodes and thyroid; does not preserve tissue architecture.
Core biopsy — wider cutting needle (e.g. 18G) yields a tissue core for histology, preserving architecture for tumour typing, immunohistochemistry and molecular markers. Usually preferred for solid organ and tumour characterisation.
Need to type a solid tumour / molecular markers→Core biopsy (histology) preferred over FNA
2Choosing imaging guidance

Modality is matched to the lesion — the aim is a safe, reproducible trajectory with continuous or confirmed needle-tip visualisation.

🔊Ultrasound
Real-time, no radiation; ideal for superficial/palpable lesions, liver, kidney, nodes — lets you avoid vessels with colour Doppler.
🖥️CT
For deep, retroperitoneal, lung and bone lesions; precise trajectory planning but slower and no live imaging.
🧲MRI / fluoroscopy
Occasional use — MRI for lesions only conspicuous on MR; fluoroscopy for some bone lesions.
Superficial vascular target, want to avoid vessels live→Ultrasound with Doppler
Deep or lung lesion→CT guidance
📷 Image placeholder — CT-guided lung biopsy showing coaxial needle tip within a peripheral pulmonary nodule, planned trajectory crossing minimal aerated lung.
3Technique
Plan a safe trajectory — shortest safe path avoiding vessels, bowel, gallbladder and pleura; cross as little normal parenchyma as possible.
Position & asepsis — position patient, clean and drape, infiltrate local anaesthetic to the capsule/pleura.
Coaxial technique — place a guiding/introducer needle to the lesion edge, then pass the cutting needle through it to take several cores without repeat punctures, reducing seeding and passes.
Confirm & send — confirm needle-tip position on imaging, send cores in formalin (histology) or saline for microbiology; a plug/gel may seal the track.
4Pre-procedure checks, complications & aftercare

Before: valid consent; confirm the lesion and approach on recent imaging; check and correct coagulation — INR/clotting, platelets — and stop/withhold anticoagulants and antiplatelets per protocol (e.g. warfarin, DOACs, clopidogrel), correcting deranged values before proceeding.

🩸Bleeding / haematoma
Commonest serious risk — mitigated by correcting clotting, coaxial single-track, avoiding vessels.
🫁Pneumothorax
Key risk of lung biopsy; minimise pleural passes; may need aspiration or chest drain.
🌱Tumour track seeding
Rare; coaxial technique limits deposition of malignant cells along the track.
🦠Infection / pain
Infection uncommon with asepsis; also pain and injury to adjacent structures.

After: observe (bed rest, monitor obs) for delayed bleeding; post-biopsy CXR after lung biopsy to exclude/track pneumothorax before discharge; give safety-net advice.

Breathlessness / pleuritic pain after lung biopsy→Suspect pneumothorax — CXR, may need drain
🚩 Uncorrected coagulopathy or antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy sharply raises bleeding risk — always check INR/clotting and platelets and pause these drugs (with a management plan) before percutaneous biopsy.
🎓 Core biopsy (histology) is preferred over FNA for typing solid tumours because it preserves tissue architecture and permits immunohistochemistry and molecular testing; pneumothorax is the classic examinable complication of CT-guided lung biopsy, mandating a post-procedure CXR.

Transjugular liver biopsy (TJLB) obtains liver tissue through the venous system rather than across the skin and capsule. It is the biopsy of choice when the percutaneous route is unsafe — because the needle stays inside the vasculature, any bleeding drains back into the hepatic vein rather than into the peritoneum. It also permits simultaneous measurement of the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) to quantify portal hypertension.

🩸Coagulopathy
Deranged clotting (e.g. prolonged INR) where percutaneous bleeding risk is unacceptable.
🧫Thrombocytopenia
Low platelets — venous drainage of any bleed makes TJLB safer than a percutaneous approach.
💧Ascites
Fluid separates the liver from the abdominal wall and tamponades poorly, so percutaneous biopsy is hazardous.
📈HVPG needed
Allows pressure gradient measurement to grade portal hypertension in the same sitting.
1Confirm the indication

TJLB is selected when the percutaneous route is contraindicated by a high bleeding risk or when portal pressures are required. The rationale is that bleeding from a transvenous needle track decompresses into the hepatic vein, not the peritoneal cavity.

Coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia or ascites needing tissue→Choose transjugular over percutaneous biopsy
Diffuse parenchymal disease (e.g. suspected cirrhosis, hepatitis) rather than a focal lesion.
Fulminant liver failure or fibrosis staging where HVPG adds value.
2Pre-procedure preparation

Obtain informed consent covering bleeding, arrhythmia and non-diagnostic sampling. Even though the route is safer, still check platelets and coagulation and give support — platelet transfusion and/or fresh frozen plasma (FFP) — to correct severe derangement. Attach ECG monitoring, as the catheter will transit the right atrium.

Full blood count and clotting screen (platelets, INR/PT).
IV access, continuous ECG and pulse oximetry; supine positioning.
3Access and catheter navigation

Under ultrasound guidance, the right internal jugular vein is punctured and a sheath placed. Under fluoroscopy the catheter is advanced through the superior vena cava (SVC) → right atrium → inferior vena cava (IVC) and into a hepatic vein (usually the right).

Ultrasound for the neck puncture; fluoroscopy for catheter tracking.
Contrast venogram or wedged pressure confirms correct hepatic vein position.
📷 Image placeholder — fluoroscopic image of the biopsy set within the right hepatic vein, catheter tracking SVC → RA → IVC.
4Tissue sampling and HVPG

A covered biopsy needle is advanced through the hepatic vein wall into the liver parenchyma and fired to take cores; several passes are usually taken. If indicated, free and wedged (balloon-occluded) hepatic venous pressures are recorded to calculate the HVPG before the sheath is removed and neck haemostasis achieved.

HVPG ≥ 10 mmHg→Clinically significant portal hypertension
🚩 The catheter sits in the right atrium during navigation — watch continuous ECG for arrhythmia. Capsular perforation causing intraperitoneal bleeding is rare but recognised; carotid puncture or neck haematoma can complicate jugular access.
🎓 The core trade-off: TJLB samples are typically smaller and more fragmented than percutaneous cores, so the safety benefit is bought at the cost of a slightly higher non-diagnostic rate.

Tumour ablation is the image-guided percutaneous destruction of a focal tumour in situ, using thermal energy (heat or cold) delivered through a needle-electrode or probe placed directly into the lesion under imaging guidance. It offers a minimally-invasive, organ-sparing alternative to surgical resection and is often curative for small tumours, particularly in patients unfit for or awaiting surgery.

🔥Radiofrequency (RFA)
Alternating current → ionic agitation → frictional heat → coagulative necrosis. Well-established, cheap; more limited by heat-sink and charring.
📡Microwave (MWA)
Electromagnetic field agitates water molecules. Faster, hotter, larger zones, less affected by heat-sink; good near vessels.
❄️Cryoablation
Freeze–thaw cycles form intracellular ice crystals → cell death. Visible ice-ball on CT; less painful — ideal for bone mets and renal tumours.
1Indications & patient selection
Liver: small hepatocellular carcinoma (curative for very early HCC, especially if unfit for resection or bridging to transplant); colorectal liver metastases.
Kidney: small (≤4 cm, T1a) renal cell carcinoma, particularly in elderly/comorbid patients.
Lung: primary or oligometastatic lung tumours in non-surgical candidates.
Bone: painful bone metastases (palliation); osteoid osteoma — RFA is the treatment of choice.
Very early HCC, unfit for surgery→Thermal ablation can be curative
2Pre-procedure preparation
Informed consent; multidisciplinary team (MDT) confirmation of suitability and cross-sectional imaging planning.
Coagulation screen — check INR and platelets; correct coagulopathy and withhold/bridge anticoagulants and antiplatelets per protocol.
Fasting for sedation/anaesthesia; IV access; group & save if bleeding risk.
Performed under conscious sedation or general anaesthesia depending on site and modality.
3Technique & imaging guidance
Ultrasound or CT guidance is used to place the probe/electrode percutaneously into the centre of the tumour.
Energy is delivered to ablate the whole lesion plus a margin (typically ~5–10 mm of surrounding normal tissue) to destroy microscopic spread.
Cryoablation produces a visible ice-ball allowing real-time monitoring of the ablation zone; heat modalities are timed to preset protocols.
The needle track may be cauterised on withdrawal to reduce bleeding and tumour seeding.
Tumour abutting a large vessel→HEAT-SINK effect — flowing blood carries heat away, limiting the ablation zone (favours MWA)
📷 Image placeholder — CT showing an ablation probe within a hepatic lesion with the developing low-density ablation zone/ice-ball.
4Complications & post-procedure care
🩸Bleeding
Haemorrhage from probe track or vascular organ; mitigated by coagulation checks and track cauterisation.
⚠️Collateral injury
Thermal damage to adjacent bowel, bile duct or nerves; hydrodissection can protect at-risk structures.
🌡️Post-ablation syndrome
Self-limiting low-grade fever, malaise and pain for a few days after large-volume ablation.
🫁Pneumothorax
Risk with lung ablation; may need aspiration or chest drain.
🌱Tumour seeding
Rare implantation of tumour cells along the needle track.
Post-procedure observation, analgesia and monitoring of vital signs; imaging follow-up at intervals to confirm complete ablation and detect residual/recurrent disease.
🚩 Beware the HEAT-SINK effect: tumours adjacent to large vessels may be incompletely ablated, leaving viable tumour and risking local recurrence — consider microwave ablation, which resists heat-sink better than RFA.
🎓 Osteoid osteoma: percutaneous CT-guided RFA of the nidus is the first-line treatment of choice, giving rapid, durable relief of the classic night pain that responds to NSAIDs.

Vertebral augmentation is a percutaneous, image-guided procedure in which polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) bone cement is injected into a fractured vertebral body to relieve pain and mechanically stabilise the fracture. In vertebroplasty cement is injected directly through a transpedicular needle; in kyphoplasty an inflatable balloon (bone tamp) first creates a cavity and partially restores vertebral height before cement is delivered at lower pressure. The main patients are those with painful osteoporotic compression fractures refractory to conservative care, or pathological (malignant) fractures from myeloma or metastases.

1Indications & patient selection
Painful osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture refractory to several weeks of conservative management (analgesia, bracing, mobilisation).
Pathological / malignant fractures — multiple myeloma, vertebral metastases — for pain and stabilisation.
Selection is critical: benefit correlates with an acute, unhealed fracture, so imaging must confirm the level is the active pain generator.
Marrow oedema on STIR/T2 MRI at the fracture level→Acute, unhealed fracture — likely to respond to augmentation
🎓 Evidence is debated: some sham-controlled trials for osteoporotic fractures were negative, so careful selection (acute oedematous fracture, correlated pain) matters more than the fracture alone.
2Pre-procedure work-up
MRI to confirm acute oedematous fracture (marrow oedema = acute) and to exclude infection (discitis/osteomyelitis) and cord compression.
Exclude active infection — a contraindication (introducing cement into an infected vertebra risks seeding).
Check coagulation: correct INR (target ≤ 1.5) and platelets (≥ 50 × 10⁹/L); stop/bridge anticoagulants per local protocol.
Informed consent (including cement leak and embolism), IV access, fasting per sedation protocol, and antibiotic prophylaxis.
📷 Image placeholder — sagittal STIR MRI showing high-signal marrow oedema within a collapsed vertebral body confirming an acute fracture.
3Technique & guidance
Patient prone, local anaesthetic ± conscious sedation; performed under biplane fluoroscopy (± CT for complex/anatomically difficult levels).
A bevelled needle is advanced transpedicularly into the anterior third of the vertebral body under continuous fluoroscopic control.
Kyphoplasty: a balloon tamp is inflated to create a cavity and partially restore height, then withdrawn; cement is injected at lower pressure into the cavity.
Vertebroplasty: viscous PMMA is injected directly under real-time ("live") fluoroscopy, watching cement fill and immediately stopping if it tracks toward the canal or veins.
Cement seen tracking posteriorly toward the spinal canal or into paravertebral veins→Stop injection immediately — impending leak/embolism
4Complications & post-procedure care
☢️Cement leak (canal)
Extravasation into the spinal canal / neural foramen → cord or nerve-root compression; the most feared complication.
🫁Pulmonary cement embolism
Cement enters paravertebral veins and embolises to the lungs; mitigated by viscous cement and live fluoroscopy.
🦴Adjacent-level fracture
Increased stiffness of the augmented level may predispose to new fractures at neighbouring vertebrae.
🦠Infection & bleeding
Osteomyelitis/discitis and puncture-site haematoma; reduced by asepsis, antibiotic prophylaxis and coagulation correction.
🚩 New leg weakness, saddle anaesthesia, sphincter disturbance, or unexplained hypoxia/dyspnoea after the procedure suggests canal cement leak or pulmonary cement embolism — urgent imaging and specialist review.
Bed rest lying supine for 1–2 hours while cement cures fully; monitor neurology and puncture site.
Early mobilisation thereafter, ongoing osteoporosis management (bone-protection therapy) to reduce future fractures.

A Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt (TIPS) creates a low-resistance channel within the liver connecting the high-pressure portal vein to a low-pressure hepatic vein. A covered stent holds this tract open, allowing portal blood to bypass the diseased sinusoidal bed and decompress the portal system in portal hypertension. The trade-off is that blood shunted past the hepatocytes is no longer detoxified, so the defining downside is new or worsening hepatic encephalopathy.

🩸Refractory variceal bleeding
Recurrent oesophageal/gastric variceal haemorrhage not controlled by endoscopic band ligation + vasoactive drugs.
💧Refractory ascites
Diuretic-resistant or diuretic-intractable ascites needing repeated large-volume paracentesis; also hepatic hydrothorax.
🧠Hepatic encephalopathy
Key complication: shunted blood bypasses hepatic detoxification → hyperammonaemia and new/worsening encephalopathy.
🫀Cardiac overload
Sudden increase in venous return (preload) can precipitate right heart failure — screen the heart first.
1Indications & patient selection

TIPS is a portal-decompression procedure for the complications of portal hypertension when first-line therapy fails.

Secondary prevention of refractory/recurrent variceal bleeding (oesophageal or gastric) despite endoscopy + drugs.
Increasingly, early (pre-emptive) TIPS in high-risk acute variceal bleeds.
Refractory ascites and hepatic hydrothorax requiring frequent drainage.
Assess liver reserve with Child-Pugh and MELD; the higher the MELD, the higher the peri-procedural mortality.
Variceal bleed uncontrolled after banding + terlipressin→Rescue/salvage TIPS to decompress the portal system
2Pre-procedure work-up
Consent for shunt creation and its main risk — hepatic encephalopathy.
Check coagulation (INR) and platelets; correct significant coagulopathy as needed.
Cross-sectional imaging (Doppler US ± CT/MRI) to confirm a patent portal vein and map the venous anatomy.
Transthoracic echo to exclude heart failure and pulmonary hypertension before adding preload.
Fasted patient; often performed under sedation or general anaesthesia; peri-procedural antibiotic prophylaxis.
3Technique
Access: right internal jugular vein puncture under ultrasound guidance.
Catheter advanced via SVC → right atrium → IVC into a hepatic vein (usually the right).
A curved needle is passed through the liver parenchyma from the hepatic vein into a portal vein branch under fluoroscopy.
Position confirmed by aspirating blood and injecting contrast (portal venogram).
The parenchymal tract is balloon-dilated and a covered (PTFE) stent is deployed to bridge hepatic vein to portal vein.
The portosystemic pressure gradient is measured before and after; aim to reduce it (target <12 mmHg, or by ≥50%).
📷 Image placeholder — fluoroscopic portal venogram showing the covered stent bridging the right hepatic vein and portal vein branch.
4Complications & post-procedure care
Hepatic encephalopathy (the major downside) — managed with lactulose/rifaximin; severe cases may need shunt reduction.
Stent stenosis/thrombosis — monitored with surveillance Doppler US; covered stents have improved patency.
Hepatic ischaemia / acute liver failure from diverting portal inflow away from hepatocytes.
Bleeding — capsular puncture or intraperitoneal haemorrhage from the transhepatic pass.
Cardiac decompensation from the rise in preload.
Confusion, asterixis & disorientation days after TIPS→New hepatic encephalopathy — check ammonia, start lactulose
🚩 Absolute/relative contraindications: severe hepatic encephalopathy, heart failure or pulmonary hypertension, severe liver failure (high MELD), polycystic liver disease, and right heart failure. Screen the heart and liver reserve before committing.
🎓 TIPS lowers the portosystemic gradient but raises encephalopathy risk — success is judged by a gradient reduced to <12 mmHg, while the classic exam complication is new/worsening confusion because blood bypasses the liver's detoxification.
